articles.headline: Amphibious robot uses origami wheels to morph between terrestrial and aquatic locomotion
articles.why_this_matters: This work addresses the challenge of terrain adaptability in unstructured environments by using reconfigurable geometry to bridge the gap between terrestrial and aquatic locomotion.

summary.hook: The robot changes its wheel geometry mid-drive to switch from a high-efficiency rolling mode on firm soil to a high-traction paddle mode in deep mud and water.
summary.what_it_does: A mobile platform traverses heterogeneous swamp environments by mechanically morphing its 3D-printed origami wheels to adjust diameter, width, and fin orientation via a single input.
summary.key_idea: A telescopic drive shaft decouples torque transmission from axial reconfiguration, allowing the wheel to expand or contract while simultaneously driving the robot forward.
summary.core_challenge: Fixed-geometry wheels suffer from high sinkage and slip in soft, deformable swamp soils while simultaneously lacking the surface area required for efficient propulsion in water.
summary.key_assumption: Removes the assumption that a single wheel geometry can optimize for both low rolling resistance on firm ground and high shear engagement on soft, saturated terrain.
summary.result: Expanded wheels reduced slip and hub sinkage in sand and increased speed in water, while contracted wheels improved energy efficiency by reducing rolling resistance on firm soil and mud.
summary.what_it_enables: Autonomous ecological monitoring in complex, multi-terrain wetlands where robots previously required human intervention to navigate transitions between land and water.
summary.tldr: Morphing origami wheels allow a robot to switch between efficient rolling and high-traction paddling for swamp navigation.

flow.flow_title: Origami-Inspired Morphing Wheels for Amphibious Swamp Robots

blocks.heading: Swamp Terrain Challenges
blocks.body: Robots in wetlands must navigate diverse surfaces like firm soil, deep mud, and water. Fixed-geometry wheels struggle because they cannot adapt to these varying levels of support and traction.
blocks.detail: Soft ground often causes wheels to sink or slip, while firm ground requires low rolling resistance for efficiency.

blocks.heading: Origami Morphing Wheels
blocks.body: The MOSS robot uses 3D-printed origami wheels that change their diameter, width, and fin orientation. A single mechanical input allows the wheel to switch between a contracted and expanded state.
blocks.detail: A telescopic drive shaft transmits torque while allowing the wheel to physically expand or contract during operation.

blocks.heading: Terrain-Specific Testing
blocks.body: Researchers tested the robot across various surfaces, including soil, mud of different consistencies, sand, and water. They measured energy efficiency and movement success for both wheel configurations.

blocks.heading: Performance Gains by Terrain
blocks.body: Contracted wheels were more energy-efficient on firm soil and light mud, while expanded wheels performed better in deep mud, sand, and water by reducing sinkage and slip.
blocks.detail: In a transition test moving from soil to mud to water, the robot successfully completed 8 out of 10 trials.

blocks.heading: Adaptive Environmental Monitoring
blocks.body: This design enables a single robot to handle complex, changing environments without needing to swap hardware. It provides a path for more reliable, long-term ecological surveying in sensitive habitats.

flow.key_takeaway: Origami-inspired morphing wheels allow a single robot to adapt its geometry to maintain efficiency and traction across both terrestrial and aquatic swamp environments.

articles.headline: Iterative Behavior Tree refinement using visual feedback and verbal critique
articles.why_this_matters: You should care about this if you are interested in how LLMs can move beyond open-loop generation to perform closed-loop, vision-informed reasoning for complex task sequences.

summary.hook: The robot learns to fix its own planning failures by reading a text-based critique of its visual execution logs, effectively treating its own Behavior Tree as a piece of code to be debugged.
summary.what_it_does: A mobile robot autonomously updates its task-level Behavior Tree policy by interpreting structured natural-language feedback generated by a Vision-Language Model critic after failed execution attempts.
summary.key_idea: Verbal Reinforcement Learning (a process where an LLM actor modifies symbolic policy structures based on textual error reports) applied to Behavior Trees using visual execution traces as the primary source of diagnostic data.
summary.core_challenge: Existing task-level planners fail in stochastic real-world environments because they cannot distinguish between hardware-induced execution errors and fundamental flaws in the high-level logic.
summary.key_assumption: Removes the requirement for gradient-based optimization of sub-symbolic policies, assuming instead that task-level failures can be effectively diagnosed and corrected through symbolic manipulation of Behavior Trees.
summary.result: Achieved stable policy convergence in physical object rearrangement tasks by correctly attributing failure causes, outperforming systems that rely solely on scalar reward signals.
summary.tldr: Robot refines its Behavior Tree by having a VLM critic explain execution failures in text for the LLM actor.

flow.flow_title: Improving Robot Task Planning Using Verbal Reinforcement Learning

blocks.heading: Unreliable Robot Task Execution
blocks.body: Robots often fail in real-world environments due to unexpected obstacles or hardware errors. Traditional planning methods are hard to tune and struggle to adapt when things go wrong.
blocks.detail: Standard reinforcement learning creates 'black-box' policies that are difficult for humans to debug or interpret when a robot fails.

blocks.heading: Verbal Reinforcement Learning
blocks.body: VersualRL uses a language model to act and a vision-language model to critique performance. Instead of math-heavy updates, the robot receives natural language feedback to improve its task plan.
blocks.detail: The robot uses Behavior Trees (a modular way to organize robot actions) which are updated based on the critique.

blocks.heading: Closed-Loop Visual Feedback
blocks.body: The system watches the robot perform a task and analyzes visual snapshots alongside the execution log. It identifies exactly why a step failed, such as a localization error or a planning mistake.
blocks.detail: This allows the system to distinguish between a hardware failure and a bad plan, which a simple success/fail score cannot do.

blocks.heading: Causal Attribution Over Perception
blocks.body: Experiments show that correctly identifying the cause of a failure is more important than perfect object detection. Even with imperfect vision, the robot adapts successfully if the reasoning is sound.

blocks.heading: Stable Policy Improvement
blocks.body: By using structured language feedback, the robot improves its behavior without needing complex gradient-based optimization. This makes robot planning more transparent and easier to deploy in changing environments.

blocks.heading: Future Scaling and Open-Source
blocks.body: The team plans to test the system in more complex environments with new robot bodies. They also aim to develop fully open-source versions of the critic model.

flow.key_takeaway: Robots can learn to fix their own task plans by using language models to analyze visual feedback and provide structured, human-readable critiques.

articles.headline: Pose-VLA uses unified pose tokens to ground vision-language models in 3D
articles.why_this_matters: This paper tackles the feature collapse problem in VLA models, offering a path toward more efficient pretraining that better aligns semantic understanding with 3D spatial awareness.

summary.hook: Standard vision-language models are great at identifying a coffee mug but are effectively blind to the 3D spatial orientation required to actually pick it up.
summary.what_it_does: A Vision-Language-Action model uses a universal pose token interface to map RGB-D inputs directly to 3D spatial priors, enabling precise robotic manipulation without relying on semantic-only VQA backbones.
summary.key_idea: It replaces standard delta-action tokenization with a unified pose token representation that treats 3D spatial state as a first-class citizen, allowing the model to ingest heterogeneous non-robotic 3D datasets alongside scarce robotic demonstrations.
summary.core_challenge: Existing Vision-Language-Action models suffer from a granularity mismatch where semantic-heavy VLM backbones fail to capture the fine-grained 3D geometry and relative motion required for physical interaction.
summary.key_assumption: Removes the requirement that pre-training data must be robot-specific by demonstrating that geometric knowledge can be transferred from large-scale non-robotic 3D datasets using pose tokens.
summary.result: Outperforms OpenVLA on the LIBERO and RoboTwin benchmarks by instilling 3D awareness that persists even when pre-training on non-robotic data.
summary.what_it_enables: Future VLA models can scale by absorbing diverse 3D datasets from the internet rather than being bottlenecked by the high cost of collecting expert robotic demonstrations.
summary.tldr: Pose-VLA bridges the gap between semantic vision and physical action by tokenizing 3D pose as a universal interface.

flow.flow_title: Improving Robot Action Policies with Universal Pose Pretraining

blocks.heading: Robots Lack 3D Awareness
blocks.body: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are trained primarily on internet images for tasks like answering questions, which makes them good at identifying objects but poor at understanding 3D physical states.
blocks.detail: Robots need to understand subtle changes in pose and contact geometry to perform precise actions, which standard vision models often ignore.

blocks.heading: Granularity and Data Mismatch
blocks.body: Robotic manipulation requires fine-grained spatial data, but existing models rely on high-level semantic labels that do not translate well to physical control.
blocks.detail: Furthermore, robotic demonstration data is expensive and scarce, while internet-scale visual data lacks the necessary physical grounding for robot motion.

blocks.heading: The Pose-VLA Paradigm
blocks.body: The researchers introduced a unified pose token that acts as a universal interface between spatial perception and robotic control.
blocks.detail: By integrating RGB-D (color images plus depth information) with camera data, the model learns 3D motion priors from non-robotic data before being fine-tuned for specific robot tasks.

blocks.heading: Superior Data Efficiency
blocks.body: Pose-VLA achieves state-of-the-art results in 3D grounding and requires fewer human demonstrations to learn new tasks compared to standard VLA models.
blocks.detail: The model maintains high performance even when pre-trained on non-robotic 3D data, proving that pose tokens effectively transfer geometric knowledge to robots.
blocks.number_callout: State-of-the-art results across LIBERO and RoboTwin benchmarks

blocks.heading: Scaling Embodied Intelligence
blocks.body: This approach allows robots to learn from diverse, non-robotic 3D datasets, significantly reducing the reliance on expensive, specialized robot demonstration data.
blocks.detail: It shifts the focus of robot training from simple semantic recognition to deep, physically grounded spatial awareness.

flow.key_takeaway: By using a universal pose token, robots can learn 3D spatial awareness from non-robotic data, leading to more efficient and capable action policies.

articles.headline: Quadruped tracks and localizes markerless nano-UAVs using arm-mounted camera
articles.why_this_matters: This research demonstrates how to offload heavy perception and compute tasks from resource-constrained nano-UAVs to a mobile observer, enabling navigation in GNSS-denied environments.

summary.hook: The drone flies without any onboard localization sensors because the quadruped acts as its external eyes, tracking it through the air like a human pilot flying a kite.
summary.what_it_does: A quadruped robot with an arm-mounted camera tracks a nano-UAV in flight, computes its 3D position using segmentation masks and depth, and streams this pose data to the drone for navigation.
summary.key_idea: Offloads the entire localization stack from the nano-UAV to a ground-based observer, using a visual tracking pipeline (a combination of segmentation and depth estimation) to provide global coordinates to the drone in real-time.
summary.core_challenge: Nano-UAVs lack the payload capacity for the stereo cameras or LiDAR required for robust visual-inertial odometry in textureless, GNSS-denied industrial environments.
summary.key_assumption: Removes the requirement for physical fiducial markers on the drone, which previously added aerodynamic drag and weight to the nano-scale platform.
summary.result: The system maintains continuous tracking of the nano-UAV without markers, enabling flight in environments where traditional feature-based VIO fails due to repetitive or textureless surfaces.
summary.tldr: A quadruped tracks a markerless nano-UAV with an arm-mounted camera to provide external localization for constrained flight.

flow.flow_title: Collaborative Localization for Nano-UAVs Using Quadruped Observers

blocks.heading: Nano-UAV Localization Constraints
blocks.body: Nano-UAVs are too small to carry the heavy sensors (like LiDAR or stereo cameras) needed for autonomous navigation in complex, GPS-denied environments.
blocks.detail: These drones lack the payload capacity and battery life to run the complex algorithms required for self-localization.

blocks.heading: Ineffective Existing Solutions
blocks.body: Previous methods relied on external motion capture systems or physical markers attached to the drone, which add weight and increase aerodynamic drag.
blocks.detail: Physical markers also make the drone larger, which defeats the purpose of using a nano-scale platform for tight spaces.

blocks.heading: Offloading Localization to Ground Robots
blocks.body: Instead of putting sensors on the drone, a quadruped robot with an arm-mounted camera tracks the drone and calculates its position.
blocks.detail: The ground robot acts as an external observer, providing the drone with its location data in real-time.

blocks.heading: Markerless Visual Tracking
blocks.body: The quadruped uses computer vision (segmentation masks and depth sensing) to track the drone without needing any physical markers.
blocks.detail: The system translates the drone's position directly into the quadruped's global map, creating a shared spatial reference.

blocks.heading: Enabling Autonomous Industrial Inspection
blocks.body: This approach allows nano-UAVs to inspect narrow, hazardous areas while relying on a larger, more capable ground robot for navigation support.
blocks.detail: This removes the need for permanent infrastructure like motion capture cameras in industrial facilities.

flow.key_takeaway: By using a quadruped robot as an external observer, nano-UAVs can navigate complex environments without needing heavy onboard sensors or physical markers.

articles.headline: Morphing aerial robot uses thruster-integrated continuum links for high-force manipulation
articles.why_this_matters: This paper explores how soft, continuum manipulators can expand the operational envelope of aerial robots by increasing environmental adaptability and wrench space.

summary.hook: By embedding rotors directly into flexible, leaf-spring-based arms, the robot turns its own structural instability into a tool for exerting high-force contact.
summary.what_it_does: A multi-rotor aerial platform performs contact-based tasks like painting curved surfaces and grasping heavy objects using flexible, shape-adaptive links that double as propulsion units.
summary.key_idea: Integrates thrusters into a composite leaf-spring continuum structure (a flexible manipulator that uses layered materials to balance structural rigidity with passive compliance) to expand the robot's reachable wrench space.
summary.core_challenge: Lightweight flexible links typically suffer from unintended deformation and high-frequency vibrations that prevent stable interaction with the environment during flight.
summary.key_assumption: Removes the assumption that aerial manipulators must be rigid to exert high forces, instead using distributed thrust to compensate for the compliance of the continuum links.
summary.result: Successfully performed painting on curved surfaces, multi-object grasping, and impact absorption tasks using a 2.5kg aerial platform.
summary.what_it_enables: Aerial robots can now perform high-force contact tasks in cluttered environments where rigid arms would be too bulky or prone to damage.
summary.tldr: Distributed thrusters on flexible links allow aerial robots to exert high forces while passively conforming to complex surfaces.

flow.flow_title: Morphing Aerial Robot With Flexible Thruster-Integrated Links

blocks.heading: Limitations in Aerial Manipulation
blocks.body: Aerial robots struggle to perform contact tasks like painting or grasping because they must choose between being soft enough to adapt to surfaces or rigid enough to exert force.
blocks.detail: Soft manipulators adapt well to shapes but lack the force capacity, while rigid robots with distributed thrusters are heavy and lack environmental compliance.

blocks.heading: Integrating Thrusters into Continuum Links
blocks.body: The researchers combined soft, flexible continuum links with distributed thrusters to provide both shape adaptability and high interaction force capability.
blocks.detail: By placing rotors directly on the flexible links, the robot can compensate for gravity while exerting large forces on the environment.

blocks.heading: Composite Leaf-Spring Structure
blocks.body: To prevent the flexible links from deforming in unintended directions or vibrating during flight, the team designed a composite leaf-spring structure.
blocks.detail: This structure provides the necessary stiffness to maintain control while allowing the robot to morph its shape for specific tasks.

blocks.heading: Real-World Task Testing
blocks.body: The robot was tested on four distinct tasks: painting curved surfaces, grasping objects of various shapes, multi-object grasping, and impact absorption.
blocks.detail: These tests demonstrate the robot's ability to handle complex geometries and physical interactions that would typically destabilize standard aerial platforms.

blocks.heading: Expanded Wrench Space
blocks.body: The integrated thruster design successfully expanded the wrench space, allowing the robot to exert larger forces than previous soft-link aerial designs.
blocks.detail: The wrench space refers to the total set of forces and torques the robot can apply while maintaining stable flight.

blocks.heading: Versatile Aerial Manipulation
blocks.body: This design enables aerial robots to perform high-force tasks in hazardous or hard-to-reach areas, such as industrial inspection and maintenance.
blocks.detail: By merging compliance with high-force output, this approach bridges the gap between delicate sensing and heavy-duty aerial work.

flow.key_takeaway: By integrating thrusters into flexible, leaf-spring-reinforced links, aerial robots can now adapt to complex shapes while exerting the high forces needed for industrial tasks.

articles.headline: Dynamically adjusting weight matrix rank during training to accelerate diffusion policy learning
articles.why_this_matters: This work addresses the computational overhead of large diffusion models, providing a method to dynamically scale model capacity for more efficient training and deployment.

summary.hook: You can train a massive diffusion policy from scratch by treating its weight matrices as low-rank structures that grow in complexity only as the robot learns.
summary.what_it_does: Enables faster online interactive imitation learning for large-scale diffusion models, bridging the gap between high-capacity representation and training efficiency.
summary.key_idea: Rank modulation and a rank scheduler (a decay function that controls the SVD-based rank of weight matrices) allow the model to start with low-rank constraints and expand to full-rank capacity as training progresses.
summary.core_challenge: Training overparameterized diffusion policies from scratch is computationally prohibitive for online interactive learning, yet existing low-rank methods are designed only for fine-tuning pre-trained models.
summary.key_assumption: Removes the assumption that a policy must be full-rank from the start of training, instead treating the intrinsic rank as a dynamic variable.
summary.result: Reduced cumulative training time by up to 10% on real-world tasks like drawer assembly while maintaining success rates comparable to full-rank training.
summary.tldr: Dynamically increasing the rank of weight matrices during training accelerates diffusion policy convergence without sacrificing final task performance.

articles.headline: Humanoid robots learn to walk by following clinical infant motor scales
articles.why_this_matters: This study explores whether human motor development milestones can serve as a structured curriculum for training humanoid robots, potentially simplifying the acquisition of complex motor skills.

summary.hook: Clinical motor scales designed to detect developmental delays in human infants turn out to be more effective curricula for training humanoid robots than hand-tuned reward functions.
summary.what_it_does: A simulated humanoid robot learns to transition from lying down to independent walking by following a curriculum of motor milestones derived from pediatric assessment tools like the AIMS and GMFM.
summary.key_idea: Developmental graphs (directed acyclic graphs where nodes represent motor milestones and edges represent prerequisite dependencies) structure the reinforcement learning process, eliminating the need for manual reward shaping or reference motion capture data.
summary.core_challenge: Learning to stand and walk from a fallen state is notoriously difficult because the reward landscape is sparse and requires complex, multi-stage coordination that hand-tuned reward weights often fail to capture.
summary.key_assumption: Removes the assumption that robots require motion capture data or expert-designed reward trajectories to learn complex locomotion, relying instead on the inherent structural hierarchy of human motor development.
summary.result: The GMFM-based curriculum achieved a 100% standing success rate and walking speeds up to 1.44 m/s, while the PDMS scale failed until a missing half-kneeling milestone was manually inserted into its graph.
summary.what_it_enables: This approach provides a systematic way to generate curricula for complex robot behaviors by mining existing human developmental knowledge, potentially accelerating the acquisition of high-level motor skills.
summary.tldr: Humanoid robots learn to walk by following pediatric motor development milestones instead of hand-tuned reward functions.

articles.headline: Humanoid robot adapts to heavy, time-varying loads using online inertial estimation
articles.why_this_matters: This paper addresses the critical problem of model bias in humanoid control when handling varying external loads, which is essential for deploying robots in real-world, dynamic environments.

summary.hook: The robot maintains balance while carrying heavy, unknown objects by treating its own mass properties as a dynamic, real-time variable rather than a fixed factory constant.
summary.what_it_does: A humanoid robot, Nadia, continuously estimates and compensates for significant, time-varying external loads on its limbs while performing simultaneous locomotion and manipulation tasks.
summary.key_idea: An Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) streams physically consistent inertial parameters (mass, center of mass, and inertia tensor) into a whole-body controller, ensuring the estimated dynamics remain physically realizable.
summary.core_challenge: Fixed dynamic models fail when external loads introduce large model biases, causing standard whole-body controllers to lose stability during heavy manipulation or locomotion.
summary.key_assumption: Removes the requirement for an offline-identified, static dynamic model, allowing the robot to treat its own inertial properties as an online estimation problem.
summary.result: Successfully enabled the Nadia humanoid to maintain stable locomotion and balance while carrying 12-lb dumbbells attached to its forearms.
summary.what_it_enables: Humanoids can now perform heavy-duty tool use and object transport in unstructured environments without manual retuning for every new payload.
summary.tldr: The robot uses an online EKF to update its mass model in real-time, enabling stable movement under heavy loads.

articles.headline: Traffic-rule-regularized trajectory prediction models that quantify aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty
articles.why_this_matters: This research provides a robust approach to uncertainty-aware forecasting, which is vital for safe robot navigation in unpredictable, human-populated environments.

summary.hook: Most trajectory predictors are dangerously overconfident, but this system forces models to admit they don't know the future by embedding traffic laws directly into their probabilistic output.
summary.what_it_does: Predicts future agent trajectories in urban traffic environments by combining deep neural networks with rule-based synthetic label generation to constrain behavior.
summary.key_idea: Uses Spectral Heteroscedastic Informed Forecasting (SHIFT), which integrates traffic rules as soft priors into a heteroscedastic model (a network that predicts both mean and variance) to disentangle aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty.
summary.core_challenge: Deep learning models for trajectory prediction frequently fail under out-of-distribution scenarios because they lack sufficient data diversity and suffer from overconfidence in their predictions.
summary.key_assumption: Removes the assumption that models can learn safe behavior solely from raw observational data, instead requiring that traffic rules map to observable map elements like lane types and stop lines.
summary.result: Outperforms SNGP-based baselines on the nuScenes dataset by producing more accurate trajectories in complex intersection crossing and lane-changing scenarios.
summary.tldr: Incorporates traffic rules as probabilistic priors to calibrate uncertainty and improve trajectory prediction accuracy in urban driving.

flow.flow_title: Improving Robot Traffic Predictions Using Rule-Based Uncertainty Modeling

blocks.heading: Unreliable Robot Traffic Predictions
blocks.body: Robots often struggle to predict how cars and pedestrians will move, especially when data is limited or traffic patterns are unusual. These models frequently become overconfident in their predictions, which can lead to unsafe navigation decisions.
blocks.detail: The core issue is a lack of robustness when the model encounters scenarios not well-represented in the training data.

blocks.heading: Integrating Traffic Rules as Priors
blocks.body: The researchers created SHIFT, a system that forces prediction models to follow known traffic laws, such as stopping at lines or staying in lanes. By treating these rules as 'prior knowledge,' the model learns to ignore impossible or illegal trajectories.
blocks.detail: This approach uses a probabilistic formulation to ensure the model understands both the environment and the rules governing it.

blocks.heading: Modeling Two Types of Uncertainty
blocks.body: The system separates uncertainty into two categories: aleatoric (noise in the data) and epistemic (what the model doesn't know). By tracking both, the robot can signal when it is unsure about a prediction rather than guessing blindly.
blocks.detail: The model uses 1,024 inducing points to approximate complex Gaussian processes, keeping the math computationally efficient.

blocks.heading: Higher Accuracy in Complex Scenarios
blocks.body: When tested on the nuScenes dataset, SHIFT followed ground truth trajectories more closely than standard models. It successfully avoided unsafe behaviors, such as crossing intersections at incorrect speeds or drifting into other lanes.

blocks.heading: Safer Autonomous Navigation
blocks.body: By combining deep learning with explicit traffic rules, robots can make more reliable decisions in unpredictable environments. This reduces the risk of overconfident errors that could cause accidents in real-world traffic.

flow.key_takeaway: By embedding traffic rules into a model that tracks its own uncertainty, robots can predict human movement more accurately and safely.

articles.headline: Ultrasound-guided impedance controller maintains constant tissue pressure during probe rotation
articles.why_this_matters: This work introduces a novel way to perceive contact through ultrasound imagery, offering a safer alternative to force-based control for delicate medical robotics applications.

summary.hook: The robot uses the ultrasound image itself to detect contact, ignoring force sensors that often drift or fail when the probe tilts.
summary.what_it_does: A robotic arm performs ultrasound scanning by dynamically adjusting its position based on the visual contact point detected in B-mode ultrasound images, rather than relying solely on force/torque sensor feedback.
summary.key_idea: It uses image-based contact perception to perform adaptive force/torque taring (zeroing out sensor bias) and updates the impedance controller's reference point as the contact location shifts along the curved probe surface during rotation.
summary.core_challenge: Standard impedance controllers suffer from excessive tissue compression when the probe rolls because the contact point migrates, causing force sensors to report inaccurate interaction loads.
summary.key_assumption: Removes the assumption that the contact point remains fixed at the probe's geometric center, allowing the controller to compensate for geometric displacement during scanning.
summary.result: Reduced peak excess compression force by 69.2% compared to standard impedance control during probe roll maneuvers, limiting peak force to 20.09 N.
summary.tldr: The controller uses ultrasound images to track contact points and adjust force, preventing tissue over-compression during probe rotation.
